title: Vinted Buyer Wants to Return Because It Doesn't Fit — Do You Have to Accept?
intro: No — if the size you listed matches the size on the item's label, you don't have to accept a return just because it didn't fit the buyer. Vinted's own return page says it plainly: if an item doesn't fit you or you don't like it, you can only return it if the seller agrees to accept the return. The Refund Policy lists "Item is not wanted" as not eligible for a return or refund. But sellers report the same thing over and over — the claim still arrives as "significantly not as described", Vinted support often sides with the buyer anyway, and if you let the response window run out the buyer can end up refunded and keep the item. Here's how the claim actually works and how to answer it.
meta_description: Vinted buyer opened an issue saying the item doesn't fit even though you listed the right size? Vinted's policy is on your side — here's how the claim works, the deadline, and the reply that holds up.
author: Supervint Team
cta_text: Never miss a mispriced listing again — get instant alerts for the items you want on Vinted

body.heading: The short answer, in Vinted's own words
paragraphs: Vinted's help article "Returning an item" (help 272) is unusually clear on this point: "If an item doesn't fit you or you don't like it, you can only return it if the seller agrees to accept the return." Its Refund Policy (help 465) repeats the same rule from the other direction, under "Not eligible for a refund": "Item is not wanted — if an item matches its description but doesn't fit or doesn't suit you, it is not eligible for a return or refund under our refund policy." The same article adds that the buyer can still ask, "but keep in mind that it's their decision whether to accept it or not."

That is the whole rule. A Vinted sale is not a shop sale, there is no cooling-off period on a correctly described second-hand item, and the decision sits with you. Buyers assume otherwise because every retailer they have used takes returns.

The question keeps surfacing in near-identical form across r/vinted, r/vintedUK and the Facebook reseller groups: "buyer wants to return item for not fitting but I listed the correct size", "do I have to let her return this?", "I don't want to accept a return — what do I do?". The first reply is always the same: if the size on the label matches your listing, it isn't your problem, and they can resell it.

body.heading: So why does the claim arrive as "not as described"?
paragraphs: Because that's the only route that suspends an order. Vinted's refund process exists for items that are lost, damaged or significantly not as described — there is no "changed my mind" button that pauses your payment. A buyer who wants out therefore has to frame the fit problem as a description problem, and the easiest description problem to allege is the size.

That produces two very different claims that look similar in your inbox. The first is buyer's remorse dressed up: the listing said small, the label said small, and the buyer simply doesn't like how it sits. One seller described a buyer opening an issue for a sweater as "SNAD" and writing that it was "not true size, it's super oversized" — while the listing described an off-the-shoulder slouchy fit. That claim is weak, and it loses when it's answered.

The second claim is much stronger, and it's the one to take seriously: the buyer isn't saying it doesn't fit them, they're saying it isn't the size you claimed. A jacket listed as a medium where the buyer argues it's a women's medium, not a men's. Jeans labelled 30 whose waistband measures closer to 27. None of that is a fit complaint — it's an allegation that the item doesn't match the description, which is exactly what the Refund Policy covers. Read the buyer's actual wording before deciding which claim you're dealing with.

body.heading: The deadline that decides the case before you've said anything
paragraphs: Once the buyer submits a refund request, the order is suspended and your money is held. Vinted's return article sets out what happens next: you can offer a partial refund, offer a full refund and let them keep the item, or ask them to return it. If you can't agree, the buyer can ask Vinted to review it, and Vinted says it replies within 48 hours and may require you to act within the next 2 days — either request a return, or release the refund so the order is cancelled.

Sellers describe the timeline in blunter terms, and the wording repeats: "if you don't respond in 48 hrs from when the issue was raised she gets a refund and gets to keep it", "if you don't respond she wins". Whether the clock is 48 hours or two days, the lesson is identical — silence is read as agreement, and the resolution goes to whoever showed up.

So the most expensive thing you can do is leave the issue sitting while you decide. Open the order, press "View issue details", and use "Contact us" at the bottom of the issue screen to state that you disagree with the claim. Do that before you've gathered everything — photos can follow in the order chat. If you can't face the argument at all, pick a resolution yourself rather than letting the timer pick one.

body.heading: Your three options — and the one experienced sellers pick
paragraphs: Partial refund, full refund, or return. For a fit claim on a cheap item, many experienced sellers deliberately choose "return" and select that the buyer pays postage. The reasoning is arithmetic, not principle: return postage usually costs more than the item did, so the buyer works that out and drops it. As one commenter put it, "they'd get basically nothing back as a refund so it's not worth returning". Another spelled out the appeal: accept the return, make them pay the postage, and "there is nothing more they can do to escalate things" — because you've resolved it yourself, Vinted's automated review never gets a say.

That last part is the real argument. Refusing outright and escalating hands the decision to a support queue sellers describe as unpredictable on exactly this question. Accepting the return on your terms keeps the decision with you and ends the conversation.

The cost is time: the buyer has 5 business days to send the return, then you have 2 days to confirm it arrived as described, and your payment stays suspended throughout. On anything valuable you may prefer to hold the line and fight instead — just go in knowing you're trading certainty for the item's price.

body.heading: What a reply that holds up actually contains
paragraphs: Your case isn't "the buyer is wrong". It's "the item matched the listing", so build the reply around that sentence and attach things that prove it. The strongest single item is a photo of the size label that was in your original listing — not one taken now, because the buyer can argue you photographed a different garment. Next is measurements: a tape measure laid flat across the chest and the length is what separates a winnable claim from a coin flip. After that, anything from the brand: its published size chart, a product code from the care label, a style name that only exists in one fit.

Put it in the order chat as one calm message rather than a running argument. State the facts in four lines — the item was listed as the size on the label, the listing photos show that label, the item matches the description, and you're declining the return because fit isn't covered by the Refund Policy. Then submit the same points through "Contact us". Resist explaining how the buyer should have asked for measurements; it reads as condescension in a case file and adds nothing.

If the buyer has escalated to "it's not actually that size", the bar changes and you must answer that specific allegation. Measure the garment and photograph it against a tape. If it's a men's cut being called a women's, the inner label's product code usually settles it. If you can't show the item is what you said it was, you don't have a defence — see the next section.

body.heading: When you should just accept the return
paragraphs: Sometimes the buyer is right and the label is a liar. If the garment has visibly shrunk, if the brand runs famously small, or if you never listed measurements and the buyer's tape measure backs up their complaint, Vinted is likely to treat it as significantly not as described. The jeans thread is the clean example: the label said 30, the buyer's photo showed a waistband measuring around 27, and replies split between "the label is enough" and "they've shrunk, accept it and relist them as 28".

The other reason to accept is cost. On a low-value item, the dispute, the messages and the risk of a review cost more than the sale made. A partial refund you both agree to is often the cheapest exit, and it keeps the order out of Vinted's queue entirely.

Two things to know before deciding. You can't leave feedback on an order once it's been returned, so if you wanted to warn other sellers, that option disappears. And if you win, the buyer can still review you — commenters who won these disputes regularly mention the one-star review that followed. Neither is a reason to roll over on a claim you'd win, but both are part of the price.

faq.question: Do I have to accept a Vinted return if the item doesn't fit the buyer?
faq.answer: No, provided the size you listed matches the size on the item's label. Vinted's "Returning an item" help article states that if an item doesn't fit or the buyer doesn't like it, they can only return it if the seller agrees. The Refund Policy lists "Item is not wanted" — an item that matches its description but doesn't fit — as not eligible for a return or refund, and says it's the seller's decision whether to accept one anyway.

faq.question: What happens if I ignore the buyer's refund request?
faq.answer: The order stays suspended and your payment stays held, and the case moves toward an automatic resolution. Vinted's return article says that if you can't agree, the buyer can ask Vinted to review it, and Vinted may then require you to either request a return or release the refund within 2 days. Sellers describe the outcome of staying silent in much plainer terms: the buyer gets refunded and keeps the item. Always respond through "Contact us" rather than letting the window close.

faq.question: Can Vinted still side with the buyer even though its own policy says fit isn't a valid reason?
faq.answer: Sellers report that it does, repeatedly — including cases where the listing clearly showed the size label. That gap between the written policy and the outcome is the whole reason to engage with the claim instead of relying on the policy to resolve itself. Answer with evidence, and consider resolving it yourself by accepting the return with the buyer paying postage, so Vinted's review never decides it.

faq.question: The buyer says it's not really the size on the label. Does that change things?
faq.answer: Yes — that's a genuine not-as-described claim, not a fit complaint, and the Refund Policy covers it. If the item has shrunk, the label is wrong, or the cut isn't what a buyer would reasonably expect, Vinted is likely to side with them. Your defence is measurement: photograph the garment against a tape measure and, where relevant, use the inner care label's product code or the brand's own size chart to show what the item actually is.

faq.question: Should I accept the return and make the buyer pay postage?
faq.answer: It's what many experienced sellers do on low-value items, because return postage often costs more than the item, so the buyer gives up and you keep the sale. It also takes the decision away from Vinted's automated review, since you've resolved the case yourself. The trade-off is that your payment stays suspended while the return window runs — 5 business days for the buyer to send it, then 2 days for you to confirm it arrived as described.

faq.question: Can the buyer leave me negative feedback if I refuse their return?
faq.answer: Yes. Winning the dispute doesn't stop them reviewing you, and sellers who have won these cases regularly mention the bad review that followed. The reverse isn't true: once an order has been returned, you can no longer leave feedback on it, so if warning other sellers about this buyer matters to you, that option goes away with the return.
